nodes.summary: The Compose renderers for each markdown block the parser emits: headings, quotes, code, lists, checklists, images, videos, spoilers and AniList entity cards. Each one carries the note on what its previous shape got wrong, from an ordered list indenting itself past the ninth item to a spoiler block that swallowed every tap on a link inside it.
nodes.languageNotes: All block renderers take a parsed node and open external links through openExternalUrlOrCopy, so the sheet never needs a Context of its own.

nodes.name: RenderHeader
nodes.summary: A markdown heading at one of four sizes, with its inline tokens flattened into one annotated string so links inside a heading stay tappable.

nodes.name: RenderImage
nodes.summary: One markdown image, honouring the `img220(...)` / `img50%(...)` size the parser captured, capped in height and scaled with ContentScale.Fit so a very tall image is not cropped to the cap. A linked image opens its target instead of the artwork.

nodes.name: RenderSpoilerBlock
nodes.summary: A `~!spoiler!~` as a labelled chip sitting on the top edge of a surface. The chip is the only control: the whole block used to toggle, so a thumb resting on a revealed spoiler - or a tap on a link inside it - hid the text being read.

nodes.name: RenderAniListPreview
nodes.summary: One AniList entity a bio linked, as a card with a reserved 2:3 poster frame. The cover is passed in from a batch the caller fetched, because a request per card would spend a dozen of AniList's 30-a-minute budget before the reader scrolled, and the fetched title beats the `ANIME #1` the URL yields.

nodes.name: imageWidthModifier
nodes.summary: Translates the parser's captured size into a layout modifier: a percentage becomes a fillMaxWidth fraction and a number becomes that many dp, both of which the incoming constraints clamp. A malformed size degrades to full width rather than to something invisible.

nodes.name: CommentComposer.kt
nodes.summary: The comment editor: Cancel/title/Preview header, reply-target chip, a full-height field with a Preview toggle, and a bottom bar with format controls, a character counter and Post. It copies AniList's own composer because that is the editor people already know, and it deliberately does not own the draft - the sheet above does, so Cancel keeps the text.
nodes.languageNotes: Every programmatic edit goes through TextFieldValue.withDraftEdit so the caret is clamped to the clipped text; the format bar scrolls horizontally because four controls plus a counter do not fit a 360dp phone.

nodes.name: CommentComposer
nodes.summary: The editor pane, holding only the state that means nothing outside it - Preview and the attach dialog - while the draft and reply target stay hoisted. Send is gated on ContentLimits so the shortest comment the field accepted is no longer a guaranteed server rejection.

nodes.name: withDraftEdit
nodes.summary: Turns a toolbar or mention edit into the field's next value, clipping to ContentLimits and clamping the caret into the resulting text. TextFieldValue throws from its constructor if its selection falls outside its text, and a programmatic edit invalidates the IME's composing range.

nodes.name: ComposerBottomBar
nodes.summary: Format controls, counter and Post, plus the sentence saying why Send is off. The reason is shown beside the button because a disabled control with no explanation is indistinguishable from a broken one.

nodes.name: AttachImageDialog
nodes.summary: The attach-image step, which can only mean insert by URL because AniList has no upload endpoint. The URL is checked before Insert is enabled, so a relative path or a data: payload is not stored as literal text that the renderer cannot embed.

nodes.name: CommentThreadStore.kt
nodes.summary: One activity's comment thread and every write that acts on it - load, post, like, edit, delete - as a StateFlow-backed store. Split from the activity ViewModel because the thread has its own lifecycle and queries, and the manage dialog is modelled as state here so an in-flight edit's failure has somewhere to land and the flow is reachable from a unit test.
nodes.languageNotes: Every write folds a `repositoryResult` and re-checks that the state still belongs to the same activityId before applying the answer; replies are de-duplicated by id because a repeated LazyColumn key is a hard IllegalArgumentException.

nodes.name: CommentThreadStore
nodes.summary: The store itself, constructed with the repository, a scope, the demo flag, the signed-in viewer id and a reply-count delta callback so the feed stays honest without a refetch. A null viewer id leaves every comment without a manage menu, which is the safe half of the choice since the server enforces ownership anyway.

nodes.name: ReplyAction
nodes.summary: The manage dialog's whole state: which comment, which step, the edit draft, whether a request is in flight and why the last attempt failed. The error lives here rather than in the composer's error line because it belongs under the field that will be retried.

nodes.name: CommentsState
nodes.summary: The sheet's state, null when the sheet is closed so visibility cannot be out of step with the thread. It carries activityId so a slow response for a replaced thread is discarded, one entry per reply id, the pending-like set, and the id of the comment this session posted.

nodes.name: open
nodes.summary: Opens and loads one thread, folding a repository failure into an error row instead of letting the throw reach the coroutine and take the app with it. A response is only written if the state still holds the same activityId.

nodes.name: post
nodes.summary: Posts a comment inside the API's own 2..8000 window, appends the server's reply at the end while replacing any entry with the same id, records its id for the sheet to scroll to, and bumps the feed's reply count.

nodes.name: toggleReplyLike
nodes.summary: Optimistic like with one request in flight per reply and a rollback on failure. A null isLiked refuses outright, because that is AniList answering without a session and guessing would put the heart in a state the server never agreed to.

nodes.name: submitReplyEdit
nodes.summary: Saves the dialog's draft over the comment it was opened for, replacing that row in place. The response is dropped if the dialog has moved to another comment or the thread has been replaced while the request was out.

nodes.name: submitReplyDelete
nodes.summary: Deletes the comment and removes the row on the server's answer. Deliberately not optimistic: restoring a row and its thread position after a failure is a second attempt at the same thing, and a delete is rare enough for the busy state to cost nothing.

nodes.name: ProfileAboutCard.kt
nodes.summary: The profile's About card: the bio rendered as AniList markdown, collapsed behind a Show more toggle with a fade at the cut, plus the cover map for the bio's preview cards. The fade exists because a clipped bio with nothing at its edge is indistinguishable from a bio that simply ends.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses rememberSaveable for the expand flag and animateContentSize with the FastSpatialSize token, so scrolling past the card does not silently re-collapse it.

nodes.name: AboutCard
nodes.summary: The card, parsing the bio once per text and threading the batch-fetched media covers down to the preview cards. The Show more toggle is a bare Text given a 48dp minimum, because at labelMedium it was the hardest control on the card to hit.

nodes.name: isBioCollapsible
nodes.summary: Decides whether a bio is long enough to collapse, from the parsed block count and a character hint. Keyed off characters alone it disagreed with what the renderer actually clipped in both directions - offering a reveal that changed nothing, and hiding two dropped blocks.

nodes.name: NoBioNote
nodes.summary: The placeholder shown when a person has no bio on AniList, so the About slot says why it is empty instead of disappearing.

nodes.name: CommentManageDialog.kt
nodes.summary: The three-step manage dialog for the viewer's own comment - menu, editor, delete confirmation - as its own window. Its state lives in CommentThreadStore so a request outliving a recomposition still has somewhere to land, and busy buttons rename themselves rather than going silently grey.
nodes.languageNotes: One composable switching on ReplyAction.Mode; the edit step reuses ContentLimits.checkReply so the field and the store agree on the 2..8000 window.

nodes.name: ReplyActionDialog
nodes.summary: Draws whichever step the store is on, showing the failure from the last attempt inside the step that will retry it. Save stays disabled until the draft passes ContentLimits, and Delete is coloured as the destructive action it is.

nodes.name: AniListMarkdownView.kt
nodes.summary: The pure Compose renderer for a parsed markdown AST: a column that dispatches each node to its block renderer, plus the collapsed-block limit that callers share. Covers are passed in as a map so a document's worth of AniList links costs one request rather than one per card.
nodes.languageNotes: MARKDOWN_COLLAPSED_BLOCK_LIMIT is public because the bio card must gate its toggle on the same number this renderer clips with; the two used to hardcode different values.

nodes.name: AniListMarkdownView
nodes.summary: Renders a node list, treating a maxLines below Int.MAX_VALUE as the collapsed signal and dropping whole blocks past the limit, then recursing into centered blocks with the same clamp. A miss in the cover map draws the badge alone, which is what these cards looked like before covers existed.

nodes.name: MediaCover.kt
nodes.summary: The two models behind the batched cover fetch for bio preview cards: a key that includes the media type, and a cover carrying the title AniList already sent. The type is in the key because `anime/1` and `manga/1` are different entities, and collapsing them showed the same poster twice in a way that looked correct.
nodes.languageNotes: MediaCover is @JsonClass(generateAdapter = true) because covers are snapshotted to disk, so reopening a bio does not re-spend a batched request.

nodes.name: MediaCoverKey
nodes.summary: What identifies a media well enough to ask for its cover: the uppercase type plus the id. The type is part of the key because AniList's anime and manga id spaces overlap and a bare Int confidently returns the wrong entity.

nodes.name: MediaCoverPage
nodes.summary: The aliased batch answer, shaped as a Page connection rather than the nullable Media root field because one unresolvable id used to fail the whole response with a 404 and blank every poster on the card.

nodes.name: MediaCover
nodes.summary: A cover URL with the title that arrived in the same response, so a card heading is not built from the URL and does not read as a debug row like ANIME #1. The title is null when the media has none of its three spellings.

nodes.name: ContentLimits.kt
nodes.summary: The server-side text bounds the app writes against - SaveActivityReply is Min 2, Max 8000 - as one pure object shared by the composer, the edit dialog and the comment store. Exists because discovering a server rule by spending a round trip printed a generic failure with no hint that length was the problem.
nodes.languageNotes: Pure Kotlin with no Android imports, which is why both UI and store can call it and a unit test can reach every branch.

nodes.name: ContentLimits
nodes.summary: The object holding the reply window and the check that reports why a draft is refused, so the UI can say which rule failed instead of greying a button with no explanation.

nodes.name: ReplyVerdict
nodes.summary: Why a reply draft was refused: blank, too short, too long, or valid. A verdict rather than a Boolean because a disabled control needs a sentence the reader can act on.

nodes.name: checkReply
nodes.summary: Measures a trimmed draft against the API's window and returns the reason it fails. Trims first because the store sends the trimmed text, so a draft of spaces plus one character would otherwise enable a button for a request the server refuses.

nodes.name: clipReply
nodes.summary: Truncates a draft to the ceiling on every keystroke rather than at send time, so the counter and the text can never disagree and the reader never writes a comment the field will refuse to post.

nodes.name: TierListViewModel.kt
nodes.summary: Session state for the tier-list feature: the saved library, which list is open, the open list's placements, undo and redo, the filter, the candidate pool and the seeding pass. It exists because a tier list became a named document rather than one pair of DataStore keys, so something has to decide which document the board is showing and route every edit through one write.
nodes.languageNotes: State is exposed as StateFlows combined from the store's Flow and a session-only MutableStateFlow for the open id, so the board and the store cannot disagree. Edits go through a private `edit` funnel that pushes the previous document (returned from inside the DataStore transaction) onto a TierUndoStack.

nodes.name: TierListViewModel
nodes.summary: Holds the tier lists and the one being worked in. `opened == null` is the library screen and a non-null document is the board, which is the single place that decides which of the two screens is up, so a deep link, a restored back stack and the back gesture cannot disagree.

nodes.name: loadLibrary
nodes.summary: Runs the legacy migration first, then reads the viewer's own AniList list to build the candidate pool. Deliberately a cache hit for anyone who already opened their profile, because re-fetching would spend one of AniList's 30-a-minute requests on a list the app is already holding.

nodes.name: setLibrary
nodes.summary: Maps AniList list entries into the rankable candidates, keeping the viewer's status and the airing status as two separate fields and defaulting genres and studios to empty so a snapshot cached by an older build stays filterable instead of crashing.

nodes.name: moveTo
nodes.summary: Files a title into a tier before a given tile, or removes it when the tier id is null. It refuses a tier id that is not in the document, because a drop resolving against a stale row band used to file a title under a row that no longer existed and made it vanish from the board with no way back.

nodes.name: seedFromScores
nodes.summary: Fills an empty list from AniList scores, but only from the titles the current filter is showing, so a default-hidden planning status does not sweep in unwatched titles. The flag reset sits in `finally` because an exception used to leave the button spinning forever with no way to retry.

nodes.name: undo
nodes.summary: Restores the whole previous document rather than inverting a delta, which is what brings back the entries a removed tier took with it. The current display options are kept, because undoing a drag must not also undo a zoom.

nodes.name: edit
nodes.summary: The single funnel for every undoable change: it mutates the open list, skips pushing a snapshot when the document came back unchanged, and clears the redo stack because a new edit is a new branch. Without the no-op check, an Undo that restores the current state would make the next press take back the wrong edit.

nodes.name: Factory
nodes.summary: ViewModelProvider.Factory that hands the store, the repository and the signed-in account to the ViewModel. The account lives here rather than as a screen parameter because a userId parameter that one call site never passed was how the seeding offer kept coming back on every launch.

nodes.name: TierListDocument.kt
nodes.summary: The pure domain shape of a saved tier list: a document with an id, a name, tiers, placements, per-list display options and a last-write timestamp, plus the naming, id-allocation, carry-on selection and bounded undo-stack rules around it. It exists because one fixed pair of DataStore keys made the schema and the list the same thing, so a second list could not be expressed and every edit rewrote everything.
nodes.languageNotes: No Android, Compose, coroutines or clock: updatedAt is supplied by the caller, which is what makes 'which list was touched last' testable without waiting for time to pass.

nodes.name: TierListDocument
nodes.summary: One saved tier list as a single value that travels and is stored as a unit. Its id is the storage key and is never shown, its display options are per list so switching boards does not reset how the other one is drawn, and updatedAt sorts the library without deciding what opens.

nodes.name: TierDisplay
nodes.summary: How one list is drawn: whether titles show, whether they sit under the cover or on it, and the zoom. Defaults reproduce the board as it looked before these options existed, and zoom is stored unclamped because the valid range is a UI fact a future build must not be able to crash this one with.

nodes.name: TierTitlePosition
nodes.summary: Enum of the two caption placements. ON_COVER overlays the name on the artwork's top edge with a scrim, which is how a wall of covers stays legible when names are the only thing distinguishing the tiles.

nodes.name: defaultTierListName
nodes.summary: Picks the smallest free numbered name for a new list, comparing with Locale.ROOT so two names that read identically on the device cannot both be created. Without it every list would be called 'Tier list', which is a library of identical cards nobody can navigate.

nodes.name: newTierListId
nodes.summary: Allocates the smallest free sequential id among the live lists. Deterministic rather than random or time-based so storage tests can assert on keys without a clock or a seeded RNG; reuse after a delete is safe because deleting removes the key too.

nodes.name: mostRecentTierList
nodes.summary: Chooses the list the library offers to carry on with: the last one opened when it still exists, otherwise the most recently edited. Opening is a deliberate act, so a seeding pass on a list somebody was only comparing against must not outrank the list they were working in.

nodes.name: TierUndoEntry
nodes.summary: One undoable edit: the whole previous document plus the label to show on the button. A snapshot rather than a delta because a delta has to be inverted correctly for a move, a tier removal that dropped entries and a seeding, and the one inverted wrong corrupts the list silently.

nodes.name: TierUndoStack
nodes.summary: A bounded stack of document snapshots used for both undo and redo, capped at ten because it lives in memory for the life of the screen and an unbounded stack of full lists is a memory leak that looks like a feature.

nodes.name: TierListPreferences.kt
nodes.summary: The DataStore-backed store for many named tier lists: an index of ids, one key per document, and the last opened id. The index exists because Preferences is an unordered map, so enumerating keys would give the library whatever order the file happened to be written in and would leave an interrupted delete as a nameless list on screen.
nodes.languageNotes: The whole library is decoded on every read on purpose: a per-document cache that disagrees with disk would show a tier list that is not the one stored, and a few hundred short strings is microseconds.

nodes.name: TierListPreferences
nodes.summary: Owns the tier-list DataStore file: exposes the library as a Flow, writes one document per edit, and holds the last-opened key that decides what the library offers to carry on with. Documents are read by id rather than from a duplicated id inside the value, so a value can never disagree with its own key.

nodes.name: mutate
nodes.summary: Applies one change to one list inside a single transaction and returns the document as it was before, which is what makes undo exact: a snapshot taken by the caller can be one write behind. It also stamps updatedAt and skips the write entirely when nothing changed, so a refused drag cannot reorder the library.

nodes.name: restore
nodes.summary: Writes a snapshot back verbatim for undo. Separate from mutate because undo replaces the current state rather than changing it, and running the snapshot through the change function would apply the edit being undone a second time; it also refuses a list that no longer exists so an undo cannot resurrect contents under an unindexed id.

nodes.name: createEmpty
nodes.summary: Creates a new list with default tiers and no placements, then indexes it and marks it last opened. Empty is a first-class state so somebody who wants to drag titles by hand does not have to delete a hundred seeded opinions first.

nodes.name: migrateLegacyList
nodes.summary: Turns the single pre-library list stored in the old `tiers_v1` and `assignment_v1` keys into the first indexed document. It reads the old keys but never clears them, because a list ranked over months is the one piece of state in the app that cannot be regenerated, so a bug here stays recoverable.

nodes.name: TierListMutation
nodes.summary: One write's before and after, handed back so the caller can push the before-state for undo and tell a real change from a no-op without re-running the change function outside its transaction.

nodes.name: StoredTierLibrary
nodes.summary: Everything the tier-list screen needs to draw the library as one value: the documents plus the last opened id, with lookups by id and the carry-on candidate derived from mostRecentTierList. A stale last-opened id is dropped on read so the library never offers to continue a deleted list.

nodes.name: TierBoardScreen.kt
nodes.summary: The open tier list: app bar named after the list, header counts, notices, the board, the unranked tray, the drag ghost and the sheet host. It owns only what a visit owns - which sheet is open, scroll, zoom, what the finger is over - because everything that outlives the screen is already in the store by the time it is drawn.
nodes.languageNotes: Filters derive a visible assignment and a visible pool so hidden titles leave no poster-shaped holes while header counts stay totals; the zoom is a local saveable value written through a debounced LaunchedEffect, and the drag ghost is a sibling of the scrolling column so the tray's clip cannot hide it.

nodes.name: TierBoardScreen
nodes.summary: Composes the board and hands every decision back to the caller as a lambda, which is what keeps the screen stateless in the sense that matters: leaving it cannot lose work. The drag hint is pinned to the screen rather than to the scrolling content, because auto-scrolling used to scroll the hint away at the exact moment it was needed.

nodes.name: TierLibraryScreen.kt
nodes.summary: The screen the trophy opens: the saved lists with a carry-on card, a create button, rename and delete. It exists because the trophy used to open the board, which made 'start something new' and 'keep what I have' the same button and limited a person to one ranking of one kind.
nodes.languageNotes: A LazyColumn with stable keys per list and per section; rename and delete are dialogs driven by remembered nullable state, and the relative-time label is coarse on purpose so no timer has to run behind a list of names.

nodes.name: TierLibraryScreen
nodes.summary: Renders the lists, the carry-on card for the last opened one, the create button and the empty state that honestly distinguishes 'your library has not loaded' from 'you have nothing to rank'. It raises rename and delete as dialogs and reports every action back through callbacks.

nodes.name: TierContinueCard
nodes.summary: The card offering to carry on with the last opened list: its name, how far along it is and when it last moved. The same list still appears in the rows below on purpose, so the shortcut never changes what the list of your lists contains.

nodes.name: tierListCardStatus
nodes.summary: The second line of a library card: how many titles are ranked plus when the list last moved. Both facts together because a count without a time reads as current work on a year-old list, and a time without a count says nothing about whether it is finished.

nodes.name: relativeTimeLabel
nodes.summary: Coarse 'how long ago' for a library card, from 'just now' up to months. Coarse deliberately, and it maps a future timestamp - a device clock that moved backwards - to 'just now' instead of counting up from a negative.

nodes.name: TierListScreen.kt
nodes.summary: The single tier-list destination and host: it collects the ViewModel's state and shows either the library or the board depending on whether a list is open. It is what is left of a 1,587-line screen, split by responsibility into the board, its geometry, its sheets and this wiring.
nodes.languageNotes: One route and two screens decided by `opened == null`, so there is no navigation argument that a deep link and a restored back stack could disagree about; BackHandler maps the system gesture onto closeList or the caller's back.

nodes.name: TierListScreen
nodes.summary: Loads the library on entry - keyed on Unit rather than skipped, because re-entering must rank whatever the library holds now - then routes to the library or the board and wires every board callback to the ViewModel.

nodes.name: UpdateManager.kt
nodes.summary: The device-independent half of the self-contained updater: fetches the release manifest, delegates the byte transfer, then vets the resulting file (zip magic, package name, pinned signing certificate) before it may be renamed into an installable APK. Holds the UPDATE_DOWNLOAD_DIR contract shared with res/xml/update_file_paths.xml, because when the downloads moved out of cacheDir the FileProvider paths did not follow and every update died on 'This device has no app installer'.
nodes.languageNotes: Own OkHttpClient, deliberately not the shared one, so the public manifest is never requested with the user's AniList bearer token; Moshi for the manifest; work runs on Dispatchers.IO and every failure is folded into a result type rather than thrown.

nodes.name: UpdateManager
nodes.summary: No updater library by design: the whole job is one small JSON file, one integer comparison and one streamed APK, and a library would add a dependency plus a Play Services requirement for an app that is deliberately not on the Play Store. Kept open so tests can subclass it.

nodes.name: checkForUpdate
nodes.summary: Asks GitHub's releases/latest for update.json and compares version_code against BuildConfig.VERSION_CODE. Never throws: offline, DNS failure, 404 and malformed JSON are all normal outcomes and become UpdateCheckResult.Failed with a message that can be shown verbatim, so a failed check cannot take down the screen that asked.

nodes.name: download
nodes.summary: Runs the transfer into a `.part` file, then hands the finished bytes to verification. A transfer failure keeps the `.part` because it is a valid prefix of the release and the next press resumes instead of re-fetching the first 2.6 MB; a verification failure deletes it, because those bytes are not a prefix of anything installable.

nodes.name: verifyAndInstall
nodes.summary: Reads the finished `.part` back and only then renames it into place. Four magic bytes catch a redirect that landed on an HTML error page or a rate-limit notice, which a 200 response and the size guard both fail to notice; the signature check catches a replaced CDN asset, a hijacked mirror or a wrong download_url, and it is also the last defence against a `.part` resumed from a different version of the asset.

nodes.name: downloadedApkFor
nodes.summary: Returns the already-downloaded APK for this manifest, or null. Exists because the first update forces a trip out of the app to grant REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES: without it the user paid for the download, granted the permission, came back and had to fetch the same bytes again. Zero-length or headerless files are rejected here rather than at the installer.

nodes.name: isSignedByThisApp
nodes.summary: Accepts an APK only if it is signed with AniSequel's pinned release certificate or with the running app's own signing certificates (including rotation history); debug builds accept anything so a locally signed APK can be exercised. It used to return true for every build when the archive's signature could not be read, which is the absence of proof rather than a substitute for it, so a release build now refuses.

nodes.name: clearDownloadedApk
nodes.summary: Removes stale release APKs while keeping the one the caller is about to install. It used to delete everything in the directory and ran before the replacement download succeeded, so a failed retry left the user with nothing even though a still-valid previous APK was installable.

nodes.name: UpdateManifest.kt
nodes.summary: The wire model for update.json plus the result types for the check and download steps, and the manifest URL. The URL points at the releases/latest asset rather than raw.githubusercontent on main because a GITHUB_TOKEN push can never satisfy branch protection, the failing step ended in `|| echo`, and four releases (v1.0.15-v1.0.18) shipped while the manifest on main still advertised v1.0.14.
nodes.languageNotes: Moshi codegen via @JsonClass(generateAdapter = true); every field nullable so a malformed public manifest degrades instead of throwing.

nodes.name: UpdateManifest
nodes.summary: The only thing the app has to understand about a release, so there is no second format to keep in step. All fields are nullable because the file lives on a public URL over an interceptable network: a missing or mistyped field has to be a value the app can decline, not an exception that takes the Settings screen down.

nodes.name: isNewerThan
nodes.summary: Compares version_code, never the version name: the name is derived by string munging and '1.0.9' sorts above '1.0.10', whereas the code is the GitHub run number and is monotonic by construction. A null code returns false, which makes an unusable manifest read as 'not newer' rather than as an update.

nodes.name: UpdateCheckResult
nodes.summary: Sealed outcome of asking GitHub for a newer build: UpToDate, Available, or Failed with a displayable reason. Modelled as a result rather than exceptions so the caller has to handle the offline and GitHub-down cases explicitly.

nodes.name: UpdateDownloadResult
nodes.summary: Sealed outcome of the download step: a verified file on disk, or a reason. Carries the manifest alongside the file so the caller can name the release without re-reading it.

nodes.name: UpdateUiState.kt
nodes.summary: The updater's renderable states as one sealed hierarchy. The shapes are shaped by two shipped failures: a failure notice rides along with the downloaded file instead of replacing the state, and the missing install permission is a distinct state rather than an error because the user has done nothing wrong.

nodes.name: UpdateUiState
nodes.summary: Sealed interface the Settings row and the launch prompt both render from, so a single process-wide controller can drive two surfaces without them disagreeing about what the updater is doing.

nodes.name: Downloading
nodes.summary: In-flight transfer state. bytesPerSecond is nullable rather than zero because 'not yet known' and 'not moving' mean different things to somebody waiting, and progress is null while the total is still unknown so the bar does not render a fake zero.

nodes.name: ReadyToInstall
nodes.summary: A verified APK on disk, plus an optional notice explaining why the last installer launch failed. The state deliberately stays here instead of becoming Failed: the APK is still there, and the old behaviour dropped the file from the state so the UI had nothing left to retry with.

nodes.name: NeedsInstallPermission
nodes.summary: The APK is downloaded but the app may not open the installer. sentToSettings records that the hand-off was already offered for this download, which stops the row re-offering the same button every time the user returns without granting, and lets the copy drop from an instruction to a reminder.

nodes.name: UpdateController.kt
nodes.summary: Compose-facing state holder for the updater and the process-wide singleton behind rememberUpdateController. Not a ViewModel because there is no state worth surviving process death; the singleton exists because per-call-site remember produced two controllers, two UpdateManagers and two OkHttp pools, so the Settings row and the launch prompt each offered the update the other was downloading.
nodes.languageNotes: Own SupervisorJob scope on Dispatchers.Main.immediate rather than a caller's rememberCoroutineScope, so navigating away from Settings cannot cancel a running download and leave the state stuck on Downloading.

nodes.name: UpdateController
nodes.summary: Holds UpdateUiState as Compose state and sequences check, download, permission hand-off and install. The permission check runs after the download on purpose: the user already asked to update, and refusing to start over a setting they may have granted since last launch is worse than downloading and then asking.

nodes.name: check
nodes.summary: Queries GitHub, then rehydrates an APK this process has no memory of downloading before offering the download again. Without the rehydration the row says 'Download & install' for a file already on disk, and pressing it silently transfers nothing, which reads as a second download.

nodes.name: download
nodes.summary: Transfers the release and then either opens the installer or asks for permission. The state is set to Downloading synchronously before anything is launched, and that assignment is the re-entry guard: two taps in one frame would otherwise put two transfers on the same `.part` file and produce an APK of two interleaved downloads.

nodes.name: install
nodes.summary: Fires the system installer and records a failure as a notice on the existing state instead of replacing it with Failed. Replacing it dropped the downloaded file from the state entirely, so the pop-up vanished and the only way back to the APK was a re-check that happened to rehydrate it.

nodes.name: onAppResumed
nodes.summary: Re-checks the install permission when the app returns to the foreground and, if it was granted in Settings, opens the installer on the APK already on disk. Nothing in-process is told when the user flips that switch in another app, so this is the only way the permission becomes a one-time detour instead of a recurring one.

nodes.name: rememberUpdateController
nodes.summary: Returns the single process-wide controller. A second one would hold a second, contradictory idea of what the updater is doing, which is exactly what per-call-site remember produced before.

nodes.name: UpdateSectionCard.kt
nodes.summary: The Settings > Info 'Updates' card: one row that renders every UpdateUiState and offers the matching action (download, install, grant permission, check again). Keeps the downloaded file visible through failures, and lays the Download / Not now pair out as equal halves because natural label widths made them look like a ragged edge rather than a decision.
nodes.languageNotes: Stateless rendering over the shared controller; LaunchedEffect(Unit) only checks when the state is still Idle so reopening Settings does not hit GitHub again.

nodes.name: UpdateSectionCard
nodes.summary: Renders the update row and its actions from the process-wide controller. Carries the explanatory copy for the install-permission detour, worded differently once the Settings hand-off has already been offered so a returning user sees a reminder rather than the same instruction again.

nodes.name: StudioScreen.kt
nodes.summary: The studio destination: one company's header plus its filmography as year shelves, scrolled with lazy paging. It is a route rather than a sheet because a studio is somewhere you go (from credits, a hero chip, or another studio's titles) and a filmography outlives a sheet's back gesture; it deliberately borrows the app's single MediaDetailHost so a title opened from a filmography is the same page, same cache and same merge rule as one opened from the Library or Profile.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses derivedStateOf over LazyListState.layoutInfo so paging triggers on the list end coming into view rather than on every scrolled frame; the detail sheet and the person-profile sheet are siblings so a profile tap replaces the sheet instead of stacking a third window.

nodes.name: StudioScreen
nodes.summary: Composes the studio page and owns its three UI states (loading, error, success-with-shelves), the scroll-driven paging trigger, and the shared detail sheet. Optional repository and entryEditor make the page degrade honestly without a session: cast and crew draw as captions instead of buttons, and the sheet omits the "My Entry" tab rather than showing one whose Save cannot work.

nodes.name: StudioSections.kt
nodes.summary: The presentational parts of the studio page - identity header, shelf headings, footer, failure and empty states - split out of StudioScreen.kt by responsibility, since none of them decides what the page is. The composables are internal rather than private precisely because the split moved them into a second file.
nodes.languageNotes: Header chips use FlowRow because a Row clipped the title count off a 360dp screen; all shapes come from ExpressiveShapes so capsules stay capsules.

nodes.name: StudioIdentity
nodes.summary: Draws the studio name and the optional facts about it (animation studio vs publisher, favourites, title count). It renders nothing but the name until the studio node arrives, because three empty capsules during a round trip read as a page with no content, and it labels the company type from AniList's own flag rather than guessing from the name.

nodes.name: StudioShelfHeader
nodes.summary: Renders a year heading with its title count and a rule out to the edge. The count is in the heading because the shelf scrolls horizontally: three of nine posters are visible and nothing else on screen says the rest exist.

nodes.name: StudioFooter
nodes.summary: The end-of-list row, with three distinct meanings: an appended page failed (with retry), another page is loading, or the filmography is genuinely complete (spelled out with the count so a short list is not mistaken for a failed one). The error branch exists because a failed append previously left no trace and looked like the list simply ended.

nodes.name: StudioFailure
nodes.summary: The first-page failure state: an empty orb, a plain statement that the studio could not be loaded, the underlying message, and a retry button. It shares one layout with the empty state so the two cannot drift apart.

nodes.name: StudioEmpty
nodes.summary: The success-but-no-titles state, saying that AniList credits the studio with nothing. It is distinct from failure on purpose: an empty filmography is an answer, not an error.

nodes.name: StudioViewModel.kt
nodes.summary: State holder for one studio's page: fetches AniList's Studio.media connection page by page and re-groups everything received into year shelves. Pages are appended lazily because the connection caps perPage at 25 and rejects larger values with a 400, and shelves are recomputed from the merged list rather than concatenated per page so a year shared by two adjacent pages is not drawn twice.
nodes.languageNotes: Exposes an immutable StateFlow of a sealed StudioUiState; a single loadJob is cancelled per fetch, and a re-entry guard keeps a route re-entry from spending a request to redraw identical shelves.

nodes.name: StudioViewModel
nodes.summary: Owns the studio page's paging state: the accumulated MediaNode list, the next page number, the recomputed shelves and the append-failure message. It deliberately holds no detail cache of its own - that used to make a title opened from a filmography a second cache beside the Library's - and instead the screen receives the app's shared MediaDetailHost.

nodes.name: StudioUiState
nodes.summary: The page's sealed UI state: Loading before the first answer, Success carrying the studio, its shelves, title count, hasMore and an optional loadMoreError, and Error for a first-page failure. Keeping loadMoreError inside Success is what lets a failed append keep the shelves the reader already has.

nodes.name: Factory
nodes.summary: ViewModelProvider.Factory that injects the repository and the studio id, so the navigation can construct one studio page per route argument without the ViewModel reaching for a service locator.

nodes.name: loadFirstPage
nodes.summary: Fetches page one exactly once per page lifetime. The guard exists because the screen is re-entered from every title that opened a studio and from the sheet's own back gesture; forceRefresh is the escape hatch retry uses after a failure.

nodes.name: loadNextPage
nodes.summary: Appends the next 25-title page, refusing when there is nothing more, a fetch is already running, or the previous append failed - the last case so a scroll does not retry a known failure in a loop and the footer's explicit retry stays the way forward.

nodes.name: retry
nodes.summary: Retries after either failure kind. An append failure keeps the shelves already read and only clears the error before asking for the same page again; a first-page failure restarts from page one, since there is nothing worth preserving.

nodes.name: StudioYearShelf.kt
nodes.summary: Pure domain grouping for the studio page: a year (or the undated TBA shelf) and the titles in it. The grouping lives here rather than inside a LazyColumn because grouping is the whole shape of the screen and this way it is testable without rendering anything.
nodes.languageNotes: No Android imports; the year is derived through a MediaNode extension property so the preference rule (start date over seasonYear) is stated once.

nodes.name: StudioYearShelf
nodes.summary: One shelf the studio page draws: the heading label, the year (null for the undated shelf) and its titles in AniList's own start-date-descending order. The label is separate from the year because the undated shelf is named "TBA" rather than given a year that does not exist.

nodes.name: studioYear
nodes.summary: The year a title belongs to, preferring the start date's year over seasonYear for the same reason MediaRelationEdge.metaLabel does: seasonYear is set on anything AniList has scheduled, while an aired title reliably carries a full start date. Null means AniList did not say, which is a fact about the answer, not the title.

nodes.name: studioYearShelves
nodes.summary: Groups a studio's titles into the page's shelves: undated first, then years descending, deduplicated by media id. Deduplication is load-bearing rather than defensive - paging appends pages fetched at different moments and AniList re-orders START_DATE_DESC as releases are announced, so a title can straddle a page boundary and would otherwise appear in two year shelves.

nodes.name: AppCustomVectors.kt
nodes.summary: Hand-authored ImageVector glyphs for the icons the app needs but Material does not supply (studio tower, trophy, sequel chevrons, motion styles, composer format controls, the two halves of the broken heart). Everything is pure Compose ImageVector built in code, so the APK ships no PNG/SVG/XML drawable and no emoji, and one toolbar button never pulls in material-icons-extended for a single glyph.
nodes.languageNotes: Each glyph is a `by lazy` ImageVector.Builder on a 24x24 viewport filled with SolidColor(Color.White) so the caller tints it; several use stroke-only paths so hairlines stay crisp at 18-20dp. Sub-path winding is load-bearing: the StudioBuilding windows are traced anticlockwise so NonZero fill subtracts them instead of filling them in.

nodes.name: AppCustomVectors
nodes.summary: Singleton namespace holding the app's bespoke vector set. Kept as one object rather than per-glyph files so the naming stays consistent with AppVectorIcons and AppExtraVectors and a reader has one place to look for a glyph the UI references.
nodes.languageNotes: Kotlin `object` with `by lazy` ImageVector properties, so each path is parsed once on first use rather than rebuilt per recomposition.

nodes.name: StudioBuilding
nodes.summary: Studio / production-company glyph. The windows are cut out of the tower by tracing each one in the opposite winding direction to the body; when they were wound the same way, NonZero fill added them to the silhouette and the whole icon rendered as one solid blob. Floors sit at y = 6/11/16 so the tower and its annex share floor lines.
nodes.languageNotes: Lazy ImageVector property; the cut-outs rely on PathFillType.NonZero plus reversed winding, chosen over EvenOdd so the glyph survives someone changing the fill type.

nodes.name: SurfaceTones
nodes.summary: Three stacked offset planes for the Theme tab's Background card, which changes how dark the app's surfaces are. The previous single square bisected down the middle read as a flip/compare control instead of depth, and the stack keeps it distinguishable from Contrast's half-circle at the 20dp a section header renders it at.
nodes.languageNotes: Stroke-only path at 1.8f width so the three planes stay legible without fills.

nodes.name: MotionBolt
nodes.summary: Glyph for the 'Chill' motion style, the most energetic spring. The bolt is filled and its three trailing speed lines are stroked, the one place in this file where both belong; the earlier zigzag met at a single point and filled into a blob at small sizes.
nodes.languageNotes: Two paths in one builder: a filled NonZero bolt plus a stroked path for the speed lines.

nodes.name: HeartLeft
nodes.summary: Left half of a heart with a straight seam on the centre line, authored as its own closed path so HeartbreakScene can translate and rotate it away from its mirror and bring it back for the repair. A clip rectangle would flatten the rounded outline and no transform could separate the halves.
nodes.languageNotes: 24x24 like HeartRight so the two line up at any size the scene draws them at.

nodes.name: HeartRight
nodes.summary: Mirror of HeartLeft, the other half the break/repair animation transforms independently. Exists as a separate vector because moving one glyph's halves apart is not possible and the split has to be a transform, not a mask.

nodes.name: BrokenHeart
nodes.summary: Both halves with a deliberate gap, for the Settings action and the error screen's small counterpart to the full scene. The halves are nudged 0.9 units outward instead of sharing the seam at x=12, because at 18dp an exact seam renders as a hairline that vanishes on low-density screens - and a broken heart that reads as whole defeats the glyph.
nodes.languageNotes: Two closed sub-paths in one filled NonZero path.

nodes.name: HeartMended
nodes.summary: The repaired counterpart to BrokenHeart: a whole heart with a stitched seam. The stitch is three short horizontal bars rather than one vertical line, because a vertical line at icon size reads as a split - the opposite of what this glyph has to say.
nodes.languageNotes: Filled heart path plus a stroked path for the three bars, kept inside the 4..20 x-band so they cannot poke past the outline.

nodes.name: ConnectionCheckDialog.kt
nodes.summary: The Settings-side AniList reachability check, drawn as a modal dialog with the same breaking heart the error screen uses. It exists because a failed check is a moment, not a silently-updating row: the heart breaks, the verdict explains itself, and the only honest actions are try again or go outside. It also distinguishes 'the check threw' from 'the question has not been answered', which used to look identical.
nodes.languageNotes: State machine over `ApiStatusProbeState.ui` plus three local flags (seenProblem, celebrating, touchingGrass). Two deliberately separate LaunchedEffects: one judges the result and records seenProblem before the celebration starts, the other times the celebration, because keying both on the status let a cancelled effect leave `celebrating` stuck true and the dialog drew the repair scene with no Close button.

nodes.name: ConnectionCheckDialog
nodes.summary: Entry composable for the dialog: probes on open, toasts when a check throws rather than answering, and picks one of six bodies (repair celebration, checking, grass, no-verdict, awake, broken). The repair animation only plays on a red-to-green transition, so opening the dialog on a healthy API does not pretend there was a crisis.
nodes.languageNotes: `requested` exists so the first frame reads as 'asking' rather than flashing the broken heart for one frame from the probe's initial UNKNOWN. The failure toast is keyed on `status.failureCount`, not the message, and seeded with the count on the clock so reopening after an old failure does not re-toast it.

nodes.name: RepairContent
nodes.summary: The recovery body: HeartRepairScene plus the 'Ani-chan is back' copy, shown only when a previously failing check turns green.

nodes.name: UnknownContent
nodes.summary: The honest 'no verdict' state: the probe never produced a classifiable answer, so the dialog says so, offers the check again and leaves the heart whole. It used to fall into the broken-heart branch, which announced 'Ani-chan is confused' over a heart breaking for a question nobody had answered.

nodes.name: BrokenContent
nodes.summary: The failure body: HeartbreakScene, the verdict's headline/detail/quip, an ApiStatusCard with the evidence, Try again, and 'Go touch grass'. The quip seed is rerolled per result because latency cannot seed it - two 'not answering' checks carry no latency, so the reader tapping Try again saw the identical joke every time.
nodes.languageNotes: `remember(reachability, latencyMillis) { Random.nextInt() }` feeds `quipFor` so each distinct result gets its own joke.

nodes.name: GrassContent
nodes.summary: The 'go touch grass' branch of a failed check: a deliberate dead end with a way back ('I'm back' re-probes) and a way out ('Not now' closes), so the joke never traps the reader.

nodes.name: HeartbreakScene.kt
nodes.summary: The breaking-heart and repairing-heart animations shared by the error screen and the Settings connection dialog: two authored half-hearts that beat, shiver, brace, split and (on recovery) rejoin with a stitched seam and a sparkle. Every stage is a spring that settles, so nothing runs on a timer and the scene stops when it is done.
nodes.languageNotes: All transforms are read inside `graphicsLayer { }` so the animation invalidates draw, not layout - the first version drove offset/rotate from a recomposed float and re-laid-out the row every frame. Colour is animated toward two settled constants with `animateColorAsState`, gated by a `derivedStateOf` boolean so the glue's float does not recompose every frame.

nodes.name: HeartbreakScene
nodes.summary: Plays the break: arrive, one normal beat, a harder second beat, a shiver and compress, then the crack with the shockwave and debris. The four beats of preparation exist because one beat plus a split reads as a shape being pulled apart rather than a heart that fails.
nodes.languageNotes: One LaunchedEffect sequences six Animatables, launching the shiver and the shockwave concurrently so they overlap with the squash and the split.

nodes.name: HeartRepairScene
nodes.summary: Plays the repair: the halves rejoin, the glue seam draws down from the top dip, then a sparkle and the stitches appear. Used only after a real failure recovers - the full-screen recovery overlay and a red-to-green check in Settings - and calls `onRepaired` when the halves have settled so a caller can time a fade-out to the visual instead of a guessed delay.
nodes.languageNotes: Starts at split = 1 because the repair is always a continuation of an already-cracked heart; the glue is delayed 140ms so the seam reads as what holds it together.

nodes.name: HeartPair
nodes.summary: The shared drawing behind both scenes: the two half-hearts with their split/rotation/drop/squash, the shockwave canvas with fixed-angle debris, the glue seam and its stitches. Optional `crack` and `shiver` channels are ignored at 0, so the repair reuses the same drawing without a second copy of it.
nodes.languageNotes: Debris angles are fixed rather than random because debris that lands somewhere new every frame reads as a glitch, and the vertical scale follows the heart's proportions so the burst is a heart-shaped spray.

nodes.name: Sparkle
nodes.summary: One mended-heart glint placed by alignment offset; two instances bookend the repaired heart. Alpha is clamped even though the bouncy spring overshoots past 1, because alpha is not a place to let overshoot through.
nodes.languageNotes: BoxScope extension so `align` is available at the call site.

nodes.name: ApiStatusCard.kt
nodes.summary: A one-strip answer to 'can we reach AniList right now?': verdict icon, label, the evidence behind it and a quiet Check action, plus a spinner in the button's slot while a check runs. It exists because a bare status light is a puzzle - a red dot next to working Wi-Fi makes the reader think the app is broken.
nodes.languageNotes: Tone comes from AniSequelTheme.statusColors rather than ad-hoc colours; the loading indicator replaces the button in place so the strip does not change width when a check starts or finishes.

nodes.name: ApiStatusCard
nodes.summary: Renders the reachability strip from an ApiStatusUi: signal icon, label, detail line and either a TextButton to re-check or an in-slot spinner. The check is a TextButton on purpose - a filled button here would compete with the screen's real primary action, Sign in again or Try again.

nodes.name: tone
nodes.summary: Maps each ApiReachability verdict to a container/content colour pair. 'Reachable but slow' and rate-limited are warnings rather than successes: the request will probably work, but the reader should expect a wait.
nodes.languageNotes: Exhaustive `when` over the enum, so adding a verdict fails compilation instead of silently inheriting a colour.

nodes.name: ApiStatusTone
nodes.summary: Private container/content colour pair so a verdict's two colours cannot drift apart when one of them is edited.

nodes.name: TierBoard.kt
nodes.summary: Composes the tier board itself: measures the available width, asks the domain for one arrangement, and places every row strip, poster tile and drop caret at the boxes that arrangement returned. Holds no second opinion about geometry, because a screen that arranged its own rows would agree with the PNG/SVG export only until somebody changed a gap in one of them.
nodes.languageNotes: A custom Compose `Layout` whose measure policy walks a `slots` list kept in lockstep with the emitted children via a `check`; row bands are published through `snapshotFlow` rather than as a composition key so a fling does not re-execute every tile.

nodes.name: TierBoardHost
nodes.summary: Measures the width before composing the board and draws nothing until the first measurement lands. A layout built at width 0 packs one item per row and gives every row its minimum height, so rendering that frame flashed six full-width bars.

nodes.name: TierBoard
nodes.summary: The board's composition root: builds the layout options for the current zoom, asks `layoutTierList` for the arrangement, wires the drag gesture, auto-scroll, hint and ghost, and reports its own window position for the edge test. Zoom divides the layout width instead of scaling a canvas, so there is still exactly one arrangement at every zoom level.

nodes.name: tierBoardOptions
nodes.summary: Derives the layout options for a board at a given zoom, and drops the caption band entirely when the title is hidden, on the cover, or below the readable zoom floor. Keeping the band would have left a 12dp strip of empty background under every 25dp poster.

nodes.name: TierRowBandPublisher
nodes.summary: Publishes each row's position in window pixels for the tray's drag to resolve against, and clears them when the board leaves the composition. Reading `boardTop` as a composition key used to invalidate the whole board on every frame it moved; and without the disposal, "Empty every tier" left a tray drop resolving against rows nobody could see.

nodes.name: TierGeometry
nodes.summary: Places rows, tiles and the drop caret at the boxes the domain layout produced, using a custom `Layout` so posters stay real `AsyncImage`s that Coil can cancel and recycle. Emitted children and slots are two views of one shared list, which makes the previous off-by-one crash on drag start impossible rather than merely fixed.

nodes.name: Slot
nodes.summary: One position in the layout's own unscaled dp units, before zoom is applied. The measure policy multiplies it by zoom in both measure and place so a slot and its content can never be scaled by different amounts.

nodes.name: TierListLayout.kt
nodes.summary: The geometry of a tier list, computed once in pure Kotlin and read by every renderer: Compose, the PNG exporter and the SVG writer all consume this and nothing else. A separate arrangement per renderer is how an exported file ends up with its labels in a different order from the screen it came from.
nodes.languageNotes: No Android imports: data classes plus one pure layout function, so it is unit-testable and shared with the PNG and SVG exporters.

nodes.name: TierItemBox
nodes.summary: Where one tile sits, carrying `posterHeight` separately from the total `height` (poster plus caption). The SVG writer used to recover the poster by multiplying height by 1.5, which inflated every poster by 86% and put the caption baseline inside the artwork.

nodes.name: TierRowBox
nodes.summary: Where one tier's row sits and how tall it grew. Exposes derived right/bottom edges because the tests assert that rows stack without overlapping, which is a question about an edge rather than about y and height separately.

nodes.name: TierListLayout
nodes.summary: A whole laid-out list: canvas size, title, every row box, every item box and a media-id lookup for hit testing and drag previews. The single value the screen, the exporters and the drag's drop resolution all share.

nodes.name: TierLayoutOptions
nodes.summary: The knobs for the arrangement, defaulting to the on-screen sizes so exporters scale them instead of re-deriving a different shape. `minCanvasHeight` exists so a list with no tiers is not handed to a viewer as a 0x0 file.

nodes.name: layoutTierList
nodes.summary: Arranges tiers into rows of wrapping items, growing each row to fit its tallest line rather than to a fixed height. Empty tiers deliberately lay out zero lines so `minRowHeight` can bind: the old `maxOf(1, ...)` reserved a whole tile per empty row and left the option unreachable on every path.

nodes.name: groupAssignmentByTier
nodes.summary: Groups the assignment's media ids by tier in one O(entries) pass, preserving insertion order within each tier. Calling `TierAssignment.membersOf` once per tier was O(tiers x entries) and ran on every frame of a pinch, roughly 1,800 map iterations and 300 list allocations per frame at 300 titles.

nodes.name: coverUrlFor
nodes.summary: Extension on a laid-out list that resolves a media id to its cover URL for renderers that draw artwork. Keeps the exporter from needing the candidate list's shape, only the layout plus the candidates it was built from.

nodes.name: TierBoardDrag.kt
nodes.summary: One long-press drag's whole lifetime: the state it builds up, the pointer handler that fills it, the auto-scroll that keeps the target reachable and the ghost that follows the finger. Split out of TierBoard.kt because a zoom or caption change never touches this file, and a change to how a drop resolves should not be read between two `Layout` blocks.
nodes.languageNotes: Travel is held as a `MutableState<Offset>` rather than read with `by`, so the ghost reads it inside `graphicsLayer` in the draw phase instead of rebuilding the modifier chain on every pointer move.

nodes.name: TierDragState
nodes.summary: Everything one drag knows: which tile is lifted, where the finger started, how far it travelled and where the board sat when it began. One object rather than five `remember`s, because a mistyped key between the pointer handler, the auto-scroll loop and the ghost is a drag that resolves against a stale origin.

nodes.name: drop
nodes.summary: Computes where a release right now would land, in the layout's own coordinates, at the moment of release rather than from the last composition. The final pointer move is not required to have triggered a recomposition, and a drop that lands one frame behind the finger is a drop into the wrong row.

nodes.name: TierDragAutoScroll
nodes.summary: Scrolls the board one frame at a time while a drag is held near an edge, paced by `withFrameNanos` so the speed is identical on 60Hz and 120Hz and stops the instant the finger leaves the band. Uses `dispatchRawDelta` rather than `scrollBy` so a mutation-priority conflict cannot kill the loop silently.

nodes.name: TierDragHint
nodes.summary: Feeds the "release to file under..." hint up to the screen and guarantees it is cleared when the drag ends or the composable is disposed. The pill is hosted above the board on purpose: drawn at the board's top edge it scrolls away exactly while auto-scroll is running.

nodes.name: tierDragHandler
nodes.summary: The long-press drag gesture as a `Modifier`, keyed on `(arrangement, zoom)` because the handler closes over the boxes it hit-tests. A list that changed under an installed handler would resolve presses against geometry no longer on screen.

nodes.name: TierDragGhostOverlay
nodes.summary: Draws the lifted poster above the board while a drag is in flight, translating it by the drag travel plus how far the board has scrolled since pickup. Without the scroll term the tile slides out from under the finger exactly when the person is dragging furthest.

nodes.name: Release workflow
nodes.summary: The only CI entry point: an advisory lint job running in parallel with a build job that treats the JVM unit tests as the real gate, assembles one universal APK with the resolved version baked in, verifies it against the pinned release certificate digest, publishes the GitHub release, fills its What's new section from changelog.json and re-uploads update.json as a release asset. Every step that publishes is gated on a non-pull-request event, so a PR builds and signs a throwaway APK that is never shipped.
nodes.languageNotes: GitHub Actions YAML with two jobs and no `needs:` in either direction, per-ref concurrency that cancels superseded PR runs but serialises branch runs, JDK 21 and Gradle 9.6.1 pinned to the committed AGP pair, and shell steps that derive the version with `sort -V` rather than arithmetic because 1.10 is newer than 1.9.

nodes.name: lint
nodes.summary: Runs `lintRelease` on its own runner, advisory only. It needs the release classes to build its model, so it costs about three minutes of KSP, Kotlin, model and analysis; inside the release job those minutes sat in front of the unit tests, so a push with a broken test waited for lint before the gate had even started. It deliberately has no keystore and no `needs:` in either direction: lint is not a gate, and the release job must not cancel the annotations that justify the step.

nodes.name: build-and-release
nodes.summary: The publishing job: restores or mints a signing key by event type, resolves the version, runs `./gradlew test`, assembles the single universal release APK with -PanisequelVersionCode/Name, verifies the signature, uploads the artifact, creates the release and syncs the manifest. The release key is never declared at job level, because a fork pull request would then fail before running a single test.

nodes.name: Resolve the release version
nodes.summary: Turns gradle.properties into the tag this run publishes. If the committed baseline names a version nothing has published yet it publishes that verbatim, so tag, notes and changelog describe the same thing; otherwise it steps the newest release's patch while carrying its own major and minor forward. The unconditional +1 used to publish every release one version ahead of its notes, and a `cut -d. -f3` rebuild once tagged v1.0.60 for an APK that reported 1.1.1.

nodes.id: function:.github/workflows/android-release.yml:Restore the release signing key from secrets
nodes.name: Restore the release signing key from secrets
nodes.summary: Decodes KEYSTORE_BASE64 and exports the two passwords, failing loudly through `require_secret` when any is missing. The checks used to be commented out behind a hardcoded password and a `keytool -genkeypair` fallback, so a repository with no secrets produced a green build on every run signed with a fresh random key - every user then got INSTALL_FAILED_UPDATE_INCOMPATIBLE. Rotating the key is unrecoverable, so the branch that mints one has to be unreachable rather than unlikely.

nodes.name: Verify APK Release Signing Integrity
nodes.summary: Runs `apksigner verify` and compares the printed certificate SHA-256 against the pinned release digest before anything is published. The expected digest used to be declared in the env block and never referenced, so the step ended green whatever the APK was signed with and several incompatible releases reached users; an empty digest is now its own error so a change in apksigner's wording cannot masquerade as a signing problem.

nodes.id: function:.github/workflows/android-release.yml:Fill in the release's What's new section
nodes.name: Fill in the release's What's new section
nodes.summary: Replaces the release body's What's new marker with notes rendered from changelog.json and deletes the maintainer placeholder comment, in one line-oriented awk pass whose exit codes distinguish a missing marker from a leaked placeholder. awk rather than `sed '\|...|d'`, which is GNU-only and could not be tested outside CI, and rather than a bash substitution, which mangles multi-line notes.

nodes.name: Publish the update manifest
nodes.summary: Builds update.json with jq, uploads it as an asset on the release - the only write in the job that actually reaches users - and rewrites the version baseline in gradle.properties and app/build.gradle.kts in the same commit. The notes come from changelog.json rather than the release body, which was boilerplate identical in every release, and a silent skip here once shipped four releases while the manifest still advertised v1.0.14.

nodes.name: README.md
nodes.summary: The tour: what the app does, how to install and build it, the three-layer map, an index of the other root documents, the release-key warning, and the project layout. Deliberately short, and it defers every 'why' to NOTES.md and every rule to AGENTS.md, because a README that also carried the reasoning went stale first.
nodes.languageNotes: Markdown with a documentation index table; most links are anchored into sections of the other root documents, so the anchors are part of the contract.

nodes.name: AGENTS.md
nodes.summary: The repository's binding rules for contributors and agents, each one recorded with the failure that produced it: PR-only main, the 700-line ceiling and its two documented exemptions, vectors-only icons, spring tokens, the keystore and version/changelog mandates, the updater's FileProvider contract, and the test gate. It is the constraints file; NOTES.md holds the history behind it.
nodes.languageNotes: Markdown rule list numbered 0-9 so code comments can cite a section (e.g. 'AGENTS.md §6') and keep pointing at the same rule.

nodes.name: ARCHITECTURE.md
nodes.summary: The exhaustive specification: layer responsibilities, three sequence diagrams (OAuth PKCE, sequel traversal, updater verification), the repository's cache tiers, the Expressive motion and theme rules, the updater's four checks, the triple-version scheme, the CI pipeline and a target multi-module blueprint. Written so an engineer or an agent can extend the app without reverse-engineering it.
nodes.languageNotes: Markdown with ASCII sequence diagrams and code excerpts; section numbers (4.1, 6.2, 7.1) are referenced from elsewhere in the repo.

nodes.name: NOTES.md
nodes.summary: The scar file: why each odd-looking part of the app is odd, screen by screen, so a future reader does not 'fix' it back. Covers the title page, studio and person pages, the main bar, the profile, the tier list, the widgets, release notes, the deliberate non-goals, freshness and the disk snapshot tier.
nodes.languageNotes: Markdown organised by screen rather than by module, with a contents list; sections are linked from AGENTS.md and BUILDING.md by anchor.

nodes.name: BUILDING.md
nodes.summary: Everything from a checkout to a signed APK an installed copy will accept: prerequisites with the reason for each pin (JDK 21, AGP 9.4.1, Gradle 9.6.1), the deliberately pinned material3 alpha and KSP pairing, the test matrix including the tests that exist because a release broke, release signing and key history, the three version copies, CI, APK size and the minSdk floor.
nodes.languageNotes: Markdown with tables for tool versions and test suites; the signing section is the canonical record of the 2026-10-05 key rotation.

nodes.name: UPDATER.md
nodes.summary: The in-app update system end to end and the failures it grew out of: why the manifest is a release asset rather than a file on main, download-before-permission, the grant observed through onResume, the FileProvider path contract that once told every user 'This device has no app installer', .part resume semantics for 206/200/416, and the three checks a file must pass.
nodes.languageNotes: Markdown with a decision flow diagram; the maintainer half (signing, CI) is deliberately left to BUILDING.md.

nodes.name: TO-DO.md
nodes.summary: The prioritised backlog, ordered by value per unit of risk, where every entry states what is actually wrong, what it costs and what the first step is. Also keeps a Closed section and the two recorded 700-line exemptions, because the reason an entry existed is the part worth not re-deriving.
nodes.languageNotes: Markdown with stable §N.M anchors; code comments and IMPROVEMENTS-NEEDS-TO-BE-DONE.md both cite them, so the numbering must not be renumbered away.

nodes.name: IMPROVEMENTS-NEEDS-TO-BE-DONE.md
nodes.summary: A feature-by-feature comparison of AniSequel against AniSync at 1.3.8/3.2.1, with a 53-row priority table, a phased roadmap, quick wins, an explicit 'do not change' list and appendices of constants worth copying. Each recommendation names the file it lands in and the repo rule it must respect, and two constraints (no offline database, no Hilt/WorkManager poller) are treated as fixed.
nodes.languageNotes: Markdown with P0-P3 / S-XL legend tables; every claim about the reference app is grounded in a named AniSync file.

nodes.name: gradle.properties
nodes.summary: Project-wide Gradle settings plus the baseline app version. The 6g heap is sized for GitHub's 16 GB runner because R8 is the release build's dominant cost, and the version block carries the whole history of why a stale value here shipped an app that called itself 1.0.0 - it is what a local build reports, and VersionBaselineTest now guards it.
nodes.languageNotes: Java properties; the long comment block above anisequelVersionName is the only record of the drift the value is guarded against.

nodes.name: gradlew.bat
nodes.summary: The stock Gradle wrapper startup script for Windows, unchanged from the Gradle distribution apart from the -Xmx64m default JVM options. Present so a Windows checkout can run the same ./gradlew tasks CI runs; the real build configuration lives in the Gradle files it launches.
nodes.languageNotes: Batch: resolves JAVA_HOME or falls back to java.exe on PATH, then runs gradle-wrapper.jar with the caller's arguments.

nodes.name: update.json
nodes.summary: The release manifest the in-app updater reads from the latest GitHub release asset: version 1.5.6 with version_code 299, the release and universal-APK URLs, and the user-facing notes. version_code is what gets compared because the code is the monotonic run number while version strings sort wrongly.
nodes.languageNotes: JSON; one of the three places the version lives, and the copy VersionBaselineTest compares against gradle.properties.

nodes.name: metadata.json
nodes.summary: Platform metadata for AI Studio sync - app name, one-line description and an empty requestFramePermissions list. Not consumed by the Android app; the Gemini capability flag that used to sit here was removed with the other AI Studio leftovers because nothing on the classpath imported it.
nodes.languageNotes: Small JSON document; no code reads it at runtime.

nodes.name: ic_launcher_foreground.xml
nodes.summary: Foreground layer of the adaptive launcher icon: an elevated media frame with two chevrons and a sparkle, standing for walking a franchise forward to its sequels. Drawn on the 108dp adaptive-icon canvas with the 72dp safe zone respected, because the launcher masks and parallax-shifts this layer.
nodes.languageNotes: Pure VectorDrawable paths with aapt gradient fill/stroke attributes; no bitmap densities to maintain.

nodes.name: ic_launcher_background.xml
nodes.summary: Background layer of the adaptive launcher icon: a midnight-to-indigo gradient with a radial cyan glow and two faint radar arcs, suggesting discovery of related titles. Kept separate from the foreground so the launcher can apply its own mask and parallax to the foreground alone.
nodes.languageNotes: Linear and radial aapt gradients on plain paths; the arcs are stroked arcs rather than filled shapes.

nodes.name: ic_launcher_monochrome.xml
nodes.summary: Single-colour variant of the launcher glyph, used by Android 13+ themed icons so the launcher can tint AniSequel to match the user's wallpaper palette. Redraws the same frame, chevrons, sparkle and beacon with white fills and strokes, since a themed icon is rendered as an alpha mask and colour detail would be discarded.
nodes.languageNotes: All paths use #FFFFFFFF or white-with-alpha; no gradients, because the platform recolours the whole layer.

nodes.name: widget_background.xml
nodes.summary: The home-screen widget tile surface. Deliberately an XML shape even though the project bans drawable assets for app UI: a RemoteViews layout cannot host a Compose ImageVector, so a drawable is the only mechanism the platform offers. Uses the platform's system_app_widget_background_radius so the tile matches the rounding of every other widget on the same home screen, and a theme colour attribute so it follows light/dark where the Compose palette cannot reach.
nodes.languageNotes: A single rectangle shape: platform dimen for the corner radius, ?android:attr/colorBackground for the fill.

nodes.name: widget_cover_placeholder.xml
nodes.summary: Neutral rounded rectangle behind a widget cover while the bitmap is still loading. Exists for the same RemoteViews constraint as widget_background; it is intentionally colourless because the provider overlays a tinted rounded bitmap derived from AniList's dominant colour when one is known, and this shape is only the fallback that keeps the tile looking intentional when it is not.
nodes.languageNotes: Rectangle shape at a literal 8dp radius, filled with ?android:attr/colorControlHighlight so it adapts to the host surface.

nodes.name: widget_badge.xml
nodes.summary: The count pill on the Featured Sequel widget. Themed with colorControlHighlight instead of a brand literal so it reads as a raised chip on whatever surface the launcher supplied and stays legible in both light and dark. It deliberately does not reuse widget_background's shape: at the platform widget radius a pill this short would render as an oval.
nodes.languageNotes: Rectangle shape with a literal 12dp radius and a theme colour attribute fill.

nodes.name: widget_featured_sequel.xml
nodes.summary: Live layout for the placed Featured Sequel widget: one recommendation given room, with a large portrait poster, title, the title it is a sequel to and a count pill. It is horizontal because a widget is far more likely to be widened than heightened, and the whole FrameLayout is the tap target because the host routes a tap only to the view the RemoteViews attached the click to. Serves as the initialLayout declared in res/xml/widget_featured_sequel.xml.
nodes.languageNotes: FrameLayout root plus nested LinearLayouts; every view that the provider mutates carries an @+id, text defaults come from string resources so the host can inflate it before the first onUpdate.

nodes.name: widget_anisequel.xml
nodes.summary: Live layout for the main AniSequel widget: cover, title, a large count and a caption. Deliberately sized so the count is the thing that survives the 40dp squash — a taller stack of text clips mid-word rather than degrading, so the cover and title are the elements that clip first. The tile is the tap target with no dead margin around the text, because a layout whose text sat in an unclickable box would look tappable and do nothing.
nodes.languageNotes: Single-level FrameLayout wrapping a horizontal LinearLayout; the text column uses layout_weight so the count stays visible at the smallest supported size.

nodes.name: widget_featured_sequel_preview.xml
nodes.summary: Static mirror of the Featured Sequel layout used as the API 31+ widget-picker preview. The launcher inflates it in a process that has never run any app code, so every value is a literal and the poster cannot be fetched; keeping it structurally identical to the live layout is what stops preview and placed widget from drifting apart.
nodes.languageNotes: Identical view tree to widget_featured_sequel.xml minus the @+id attributes, with literal sample strings instead of string resources.

nodes.name: widget_arriving_sequels.xml
nodes.summary: Live layout for the Arriving Sequels widget: cover, title, count and handle in the same shape as the other two tiles. The cover sits on the neutral widget_cover_placeholder until the provider draws the entry's dominant colour over it, so the tile never shows a grey hole while the poster loads.
nodes.languageNotes: FrameLayout with a horizontal LinearLayout; the cover ImageView's background is the placeholder drawable that the provider replaces with a dominant-colour fill.

nodes.name: widget_missed_sequels.xml
nodes.summary: Live layout for the Missed Sequels widget. It makes the same bargain as the main widget — the count survives the 40dp squash while the cover and title clip first — and the top sequel's poster carries the entry's dominant colour behind it while it loads.
nodes.languageNotes: Same view tree as widget_arriving_sequels.xml; the count TextView uses 28sp bold with includeFontPadding=false so it fits the minimum tile height.

nodes.name: widget_anisequel_preview.xml
nodes.summary: Static mirror of the main widget layout shown in the API 31+ widget picker. Since the picker asks for a layout rather than a screenshot, the sample title, count and handle are literals: the launcher inflates this in a process with none of the app's code, so nothing can be filled in at display time. It is the reference for why the sibling preview layouts also use literals.
nodes.languageNotes: Duplicate view tree without ids; text is hardcoded because no resource lookup or network fetch is available to the launcher's inflation.

nodes.name: widget_arriving_sequels_preview.xml
nodes.summary: Static mirror of the Arriving Sequels layout for the API 31+ widget picker, with literal sample values because the launcher inflates it outside the app process.
nodes.languageNotes: Mirrors widget_arriving_sequels.xml structure exactly, keeping only the caption as a string resource.

nodes.name: widget_missed_sequels_preview.xml
nodes.summary: Static mirror of the Missed Sequels layout for the API 31+ widget picker, with literal sample values because the launcher inflates it outside the app process.
